stem:
What does this Go program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    go fmt.Println("hi")
}
```

options.text: Always `hi`, because a started goroutine always runs to completion
options.why: Nothing waits for the goroutine. The program does not wait for non-main goroutines before exiting.

options.text: Usually nothing: the program exits when `main` returns, without waiting
options.why: Returning from main ends the program; the goroutine may never get scheduled, so the output is not guaranteed.

options.text: A compile error, because `fmt.Println` returns values that must be used
options.why: Calling a function in a go statement discards its results; this compiles fine.

options.text: A runtime panic: `all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`
options.why: The deadlock error needs every goroutine blocked; here main simply returns.

explanation: Program execution in Go ends when `main` returns, and it does not wait for other goroutines. The spawned goroutine may or may not run before exit, so "hi" is not guaranteed. Wait for goroutines explicitly with a `sync.WaitGroup`, a channel or `errgroup`.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Program execution

stem: In Rust, an `Rc<Vec<i32>>` can be moved into a closure passed to `std::thread::spawn`.

options.text: True
options.why: `Rc` is not `Send`, so the compiler rejects moving it into a closure that `thread::spawn` requires to be `Send`.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `Rc` uses a non-atomic reference count, so it is `!Send`; use `Arc` to share ownership across threads.

explanation: `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `Send + 'static`. `Rc<T>` updates its reference count non-atomically, so two threads cloning or dropping it could corrupt the count; the standard library marks it `!Send`. `Arc<T>` uses atomic reference counting and is `Send` when `T: Send + Sync`.
reference: The Rust Book: Shared-State Concurrency (Arc<T>)

stem: Match each runtime with its main unit of concurrency.

options.text: Goroutine, multiplexed onto OS threads by the runtime scheduler
options.why: Go's scheduler maps many goroutines onto a few OS threads.

options.text: Isolated lightweight process with its own heap and mailbox
options.why: BEAM processes share nothing and talk by message passing.

options.text: Virtual thread mounted on a small set of carrier platform threads
options.why: Java 21 virtual threads are cheap threads scheduled by the JDK.

options.text: A single-threaded event loop, plus worker threads for parallel work
options.why: JavaScript code runs on one loop unless you add workers.

explanation: All four give you cheap concurrency, but the unit differs: Go runs goroutines on an M:N scheduler, the BEAM runs isolated processes that share nothing, Java 21 adds virtual threads mounted on carrier threads, and Node.js runs JavaScript on one event loop with `worker_threads` for parallelism.
reference: Go, Erlang, JEP 444 and Node.js documentation

stem:
What does this print?

```go
ch := make(chan int)
close(ch)
v, ok := <-ch
fmt.Println(v, ok)
```

options.text: `0 false`
options.why: Receiving from a closed, empty channel returns the zero value immediately, with ok set to false.

options.text: It panics: `receive from closed channel`
options.why: Only sending on (or closing) a closed channel panics; receiving is allowed.

options.text: It blocks forever and the runtime reports a deadlock
options.why: A closed channel never blocks receivers; that is what makes `for range ch` terminate.

options.text: `0 true`
options.why: ok is true only when the value came from a real send; here it reports the channel is closed and drained.

explanation: A receive on a closed channel proceeds immediately and yields the zero value after any buffered values are drained. The two-value form `v, ok := <-ch` reports `ok == false` to tell you the channel is closed. This is what lets `for v := range ch` loops end cleanly.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Receive operator

stem: Which Java class, added in Java 8, represents an asynchronous result you can chain with `thenApply`, `thenCompose` and `exceptionally`? Type the class name.
explanation: `CompletableFuture` implements both `Future` and `CompletionStage`, so it can be completed explicitly and composed with callbacks such as `thenApply`, `thenCompose`, `thenCombine` and `exceptionally`, unlike the plain `Future` returned by `ExecutorService.submit`.
reference: Java SE API: CompletableFuture

stem:
A Go request handler derives contexts like this:

```go
parent, cancelParent := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
child, cancelChild := context.WithCancel(parent)

cancelChild()
fmt.Println(parent.Err(), child.Err())
```

What does it print, and what would calling `cancelParent()` instead have done?

options.text: `<nil> context canceled`; cancelling the parent would cancel the child too
options.why: Cancellation flows down the tree: a child never cancels its parent, but a parent cancels every descendant.

options.text: `context canceled context canceled`; cancelling either one cancels the whole tree
options.why: Contexts only propagate cancellation downward, so cancelling the child leaves the parent running.

options.text: `<nil> <nil>`; a context is only cancelled when its deadline passes
options.why: WithCancel contexts are cancelled by calling their cancel function, with no deadline involved.

options.text: `<nil> context canceled`; cancelling the parent would leave the child running
options.why: A derived context is cancelled when its parent is, which is why handlers pass contexts down the call chain.

explanation: Contexts form a tree. Calling a cancel function cancels that context and every context derived from it, so `cancelChild()` sets `child.Err()` to `context.Canceled` while `parent.Err()` stays `nil`. Cancelling the parent closes the parent's `Done` channel and cancels all of its children, which is how a request's cancellation reaches every goroutine working on it. Always call the cancel function, usually with `defer cancel()`, or the context's resources stay attached to the parent until it is cancelled; `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags this.
reference: Go docs: package context

options.text: Increments can be lost, because `count++` is a read, an add and a write
options.why: Two threads can read the same value and both write value + 1.

options.text: Switching to `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` makes each increment atomic
options.why: It uses a CAS loop or an atomic add instruction, so no update is lost.

options.text: `volatile` makes each write visible to threads that read `count` later
options.why: That is exactly what volatile guarantees: visibility and ordering, not atomicity.

options.text: `volatile` turns `count++` into a single atomic operation
options.why: Volatile affects visibility and reordering only; compound operations stay non-atomic.

options.text: Lost updates only happen on machines with several CPU sockets
options.why: A thread can be preempted between the read and the write even on one core.

explanation: The Java Memory Model guarantees that a volatile write happens-before every later read of that variable, so threads never see a stale value. It does not make `count++` atomic: the read-modify-write can interleave and lose updates. Use `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder` or a lock for counters.
reference: Java Language Specification §17.4; java.util.concurrent.atomic

options.text: Pool threads run with all logging disabled by default
options.why: The pool does not touch logging; the exception never reaches a handler at all.

options.text: The executor retries the task silently until it succeeds
options.why: Executors never retry tasks on their own.

options.text: The Future holds the exception until `get()` is called
options.why: Without a call to get(), the failure stays inside the Future and is never reported.

options.text: Unchecked exceptions thrown on pool threads are always discarded by the JVM
options.why: An uncaught exception on a plain thread is printed by the default handler.

explanation: `submit` wraps the task in a `FutureTask`, which catches any exception and stores it. It surfaces only when someone calls `get()`, wrapped in an `ExecutionException`. `execute()` behaves differently: the exception reaches the thread's uncaught-exception handler and is printed. Always observe futures, or handle errors inside the task.
reference: Java SE API: ExecutorService.submit, FutureTask

options.text: `Vec<i32>` is not `Send`, so it can never be used from another thread
options.why: `Vec<i32>` is Send; moving it into the thread is fine.

options.text: The closure borrows `v`, which the thread could outlive
options.why: thread::spawn needs a 'static closure; add `move`, or use `thread::scope` to borrow safely.

options.text: `println!` cannot be called from threads other than main
options.why: Printing works from any thread; stdout is protected by a lock.

options.text: A `JoinHandle` must be stored in an `Arc` before calling `join`
options.why: JoinHandle is used directly; no Arc is needed.

explanation: `thread::spawn` requires a `'static` closure because the compiler can't prove the thread finishes before `main`'s locals are dropped, even though `join` is called. The error suggests `move` to transfer ownership of `v`. Alternatively, `std::thread::scope` guarantees all scoped threads are joined before it returns, so they may borrow locals.
reference: The Rust Book: Using move Closures with Threads

stem: In Node.js, code running in separate `worker_threads` workers can execute JavaScript at the same time on different CPU cores, each worker with its own event loop.

options.text: True
options.why: Each worker runs its own V8 isolate and event loop on its own OS thread, so they execute in parallel.

options.text: False
options.why: Workers are real OS threads, unlike async functions, which all share the main event loop.

explanation: Each `worker_threads` worker runs in its own OS thread with its own V8 isolate and event loop, so CPU-bound work in different workers runs in parallel. Workers don't share ordinary JS objects; they communicate with `postMessage` (structured clone or transfer) or share raw memory through `SharedArrayBuffer`.
reference: Node.js docs: Worker threads

stem: Put the steps of a graceful Java `ExecutorService` shutdown in order.

options.text: Call `shutdown()` so the pool stops accepting new tasks
Call `awaitTermination(timeout)` to let queued and running tasks finish
If it timed out, call `shutdownNow()` to interrupt running tasks
Call `awaitTermination` again briefly, then log if tasks still did not stop

explanation: This is the pattern from the `ExecutorService` Javadoc. `shutdown()` rejects new work but lets queued tasks run; `awaitTermination` waits up to a deadline; `shutdownNow()` interrupts running tasks and returns the ones still queued; a second wait catches tasks that respond to interruption. Interruption is cooperative, so tasks that ignore it may still keep running.
reference: Java SE API: ExecutorService (usage example)

stem:
Both channels already have a value waiting. What does this print, run many times?

```go
a := make(chan string, 1)
b := make(chan string, 1)
a <- "a"
b <- "b"
select {
case v := <-a:
    fmt.Println(v)
case v := <-b:
    fmt.Println(v)
}
```

options.text: Always `a`, because select checks its cases from top to bottom
options.why: Go deliberately avoids textual order so that one case can't starve the others.

options.text: `a` or `b`, chosen pseudo-randomly each time
options.why: When several cases are ready, select picks one with uniform pseudo-random selection.

options.text: Always `b`, because the most recently filled channel wins
options.why: Fill order plays no part in which ready case select chooses.

options.text: Both `a` and `b`, because every ready case runs once
options.why: Exactly one case runs per execution of a select statement.

explanation: The Go spec says that if more than one communication can proceed, a single one is chosen via uniform pseudo-random selection. This prevents starvation. If you need priority, use nested selects or check the high-priority channel first in a separate non-blocking select.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Select statements

stem: Match each runtime with its standard way to cancel in-flight work.

options.text: Pass a `context.Context` and stop when `ctx.Done()` is closed
options.why: Go cancellation is explicit and travels down the call tree.

options.text: Call `Thread.interrupt()` or `Future.cancel(true)`; the code must check the flag
options.why: Java interruption is cooperative.

options.text: Call `task.cancel()`, which raises `CancelledError` at the next `await`
options.why: asyncio cancels at suspension points.

options.text: Pass an `AbortSignal` from an `AbortController` and call `abort()`
options.why: The web-standard cancellation token, used by `fetch` and Node APIs.

explanation: All four mechanisms are cooperative: they signal, and the running code must notice and stop. A tight CPU loop that never checks `ctx.Done()`, `Thread.interrupted()`, never awaits, or never reads `signal.aborted` cannot be cancelled by any of them.
reference: Go context package; Java Thread.interrupt; asyncio Task.cancel; AbortController

stem: Rust marks types that are safe to transfer to another thread with an auto trait. A type that is safe to share by reference between threads implements `Sync`. What is the trait for transferring ownership across threads? Type its name.
explanation: `Send` means a value can be moved to another thread; `Sync` means `&T` can be shared between threads (equivalently, `&T` is `Send`). Both are auto traits: the compiler implements them for types whose fields are all `Send`/`Sync`, and types like `Rc` and `RefCell` opt out.
reference: The Rust Book: Extensible Concurrency with Send and Sync

stem: A single process must run CPU-bound computation on all 8 cores using threads or their equivalent in that runtime. Which options achieve real parallel execution? (Choose three.)

options.text: Go goroutines, with `GOMAXPROCS` at its default of the CPU count
options.why: Goroutines run in parallel on up to GOMAXPROCS OS threads.

options.text: Java platform threads or virtual threads
options.why: JVM threads run Java code in parallel across cores.

options.text: Rust `std::thread` threads
options.why: Each is a real OS thread that runs in parallel.

options.text: Standard CPython `threading.Thread` workers (the GIL build)
options.why: The GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time.

options.text: Many `async` functions awaited together on the Node.js main thread
options.why: They interleave on one event loop thread and never run in parallel.

explanation: Go, the JVM and Rust map their threads onto OS threads that execute in parallel. Standard CPython serialises bytecode execution with the GIL (use processes, or the experimental free-threaded build), and async functions on one Node.js event loop take turns on a single thread; parallel JavaScript needs `worker_threads`.
reference: Go runtime docs; JEP 444; The Rust Book ch. 16; CPython GIL

options.text: `defer wg.Done()` runs too early and must be called at the end
options.why: A deferred call runs when the function returns, after work(); that part is fine.

options.text: `Add` runs in the goroutines, so `Wait` may see zero first
options.why: Call wg.Add before the go statement so the counter is raised before Wait can observe it.

options.text: A `WaitGroup` can only track one goroutine at a time
options.why: A WaitGroup counts any number of goroutines.

options.text: The loop variable `i` is shared, which corrupts the counter
options.why: i is not used here, and since Go 1.22 each iteration has its own i anyway.

explanation: The `sync` docs require that calls to `Add` with a positive delta happen before `Wait`. When `Add` runs inside the goroutine, `Wait` may run first, see a zero counter and return immediately; worse, a `Done` racing a counter reset can drive it negative and panic. Call `wg.Add(1)` (or `wg.Add(n)`) before starting each goroutine.
reference: Go package sync: WaitGroup

options.text: `defer` releases the lock before `c.n++` executes
options.why: The deferred Unlock runs after c.n++, when Inc returns.

options.text: `sync.Mutex` must be created with a constructor before use
options.why: The zero value of sync.Mutex is an unlocked, ready-to-use mutex.

options.text: The value receiver means each call locks its own copy
options.why: Use a pointer receiver `(c *Counter)`; `go vet` flags this as a copied lock.

options.text: Mutexes cannot be embedded as struct fields in Go
options.why: Embedding a mutex as a field is the idiomatic pattern.

explanation: With a value receiver, every call works on a copy of `Counter`, including a copy of the mutex and of `n`. Callers never share a lock, and the increment is lost when the copy is discarded. A `sync.Mutex` must not be copied after first use; `go vet`'s copylocks check reports it. Use `func (c *Counter) Inc()`.
reference: Go package sync: Mutex ("must not be copied after first use")

options.text: After a timeout, the goroutine blocks forever on its send
options.why: Make the channel buffered with capacity 1 so the send always completes.

options.text: `ctx.Done()` starts a new timer goroutine on every call
options.why: Done returns a channel; reading it doesn't create goroutines.

options.text: Unbuffered channels are never garbage-collected
options.why: Channels are collected like any value once unreachable; the stuck goroutine keeps this one reachable.

options.text: `select` keeps a goroutine alive for every case it did not choose
options.why: select doesn't spawn goroutines; the leak comes from the blocked sender.

explanation: When the context wins, `fetch` returns and nothing will ever receive from `ch`. The worker goroutine then blocks forever on `ch <- slowCall()`, holding its stack and everything it references. Goroutines are never garbage-collected while blocked. A buffer of one (`make(chan string, 1)`) lets the late send complete and the goroutine exit; passing `ctx` into `slowCall` also lets it stop early.
reference: Go blog: Go Concurrency Patterns: Context; Go memory leaks via blocked goroutines

options.text: Always `333`, because every closure shares one loop variable `i`
options.why: That was the pre-1.22 behaviour; since Go 1.22 each iteration declares a new i.

options.text: Always `012`, because goroutines start in creation order
options.why: Each goroutine sees its own i, but scheduling order is not guaranteed.

options.text: Some ordering of `0`, `1` and `2`, such as `201`
options.why: Each iteration has its own i, and the goroutines may run in any order.

options.text: It does not compile: closures cannot capture loop variables
options.why: Capturing loop variables is allowed; Go 1.22 only changed their scope.

explanation: Go 1.22 changed `for` loops so that each iteration has its own copy of the loop variable, which applies to modules whose `go.mod` says `go 1.22` or later. Each closure therefore captures a distinct `i` (0, 1 and 2), and the program prints each digit once in an order chosen by the scheduler. Before Go 1.22, the closures shared one variable and often printed `333`.
reference: Go 1.22 release notes: loop variables

stem: Which of these Go channel operations cause a run-time panic? (Choose three.)

options.text: Sending on a closed channel
options.why: The spec says a send on a closed channel causes a run-time panic.

options.text: Closing a nil channel
options.why: Calling close on a nil channel panics.

options.text: Closing a channel that is already closed
options.why: A second close panics, which is why only the sender should close.

options.text: Receiving from a nil channel
options.why: It blocks forever instead; in a select, a nil channel case is simply never ready.

options.text: Receiving from a closed channel
options.why: It returns the zero value immediately, with ok == false.

options.text: Sending on a nil channel
options.why: It blocks forever; it never panics.

explanation: Channel operations fall into three groups. Panics: send on closed, close nil, close closed. Block forever: send or receive on nil. Succeed immediately: receive on closed (zero value, `ok == false`). The rule "only the sender closes, and only once" follows from these panics, and setting a channel to nil is a deliberate way to disable a select case.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Send statements, Close

options.text: `CompletableFuture<User>`, which is already exactly what the code needs here
options.why: thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, so the future gets nested.

options.text: `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<User>>`; use `thenCompose` instead
options.why: thenCompose flattens a function that itself returns a stage, like flatMap.

options.text: `User`, because `thenApply` blocks until the value is ready
options.why: thenApply never blocks; it returns a new future immediately.

options.text: A compile error, because `thenApply` can't return a future; use `thenAccept`
options.why: thenAccept returns CompletableFuture<Void> and would discard the user.

explanation: `thenApply` is like `map`: it wraps the function's return value in a new stage, so a function returning a future gives a future of a future. `thenCompose` is like `flatMap`: it expects the function to return a `CompletionStage` and flattens it, giving `CompletableFuture<User>`.
reference: Java SE API: CompletionStage.thenCompose

options.text: The catch block runs, because `join` rethrows the original exception
options.why: join wraps the failure; the original is only the cause.

options.text: `join` returns `null`, because exceptions in async stages are swallowed
options.why: The failure isn't swallowed; join throws.

options.text: `join` throws `ExecutionException`, which escapes the catch
options.why: That is what get() throws; join throws the unchecked CompletionException.

options.text: `join` throws `CompletionException`, so the catch is skipped
options.why: Catch CompletionException and inspect getCause(), or handle errors with exceptionally/handle.

explanation: When a stage completes exceptionally, `join()` throws an unchecked `CompletionException` whose cause is the original exception, while `get()` throws a checked `ExecutionException`. A catch for `IllegalStateException` does not match, so the exception propagates. Handle failures in the pipeline with `exceptionally` or `handle`, or unwrap `getCause()`.
reference: Java SE API: CompletableFuture.join

stem: On JDK 21, a service runs each request on its own virtual thread. The JDBC driver blocks on socket reads while inside `synchronized` methods. With 10,000 concurrent requests, throughput is stuck at roughly the number of CPU cores. Why?

options.text: Virtual threads are limited to one per CPU core by design
options.why: Millions of virtual threads can exist; only the carriers are limited to about the core count.

options.text: Blocking inside `synchronized` pins each virtual thread to its carrier
options.why: Pinned threads can't unmount, so carriers run out; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed this for synchronized.

options.text: JDBC drivers detect virtual threads and fall back to a single connection
options.why: Drivers don't do that; the bottleneck is the pinned carriers.

options.text: The default carrier pool has a single thread unless you configure it
options.why: The scheduler defaults to about as many carriers as available processors.

explanation: A virtual thread normally unmounts from its carrier when it blocks, freeing the carrier for other virtual threads. In JDK 21, blocking while holding a monitor (`synchronized`) pins the virtual thread, so each blocked request occupies a carrier, and the carrier pool is about the size of the CPU count. Fixes on JDK 21 are `ReentrantLock` or an updated driver; JEP 491 in JDK 24 lets virtual threads block in `synchronized` without pinning (calls through native code can still pin).
reference: JEP 444: Virtual Threads; JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning

stem: A team migrating to Java 21 virtual threads wants to stop a downstream database from being flooded with more than 50 concurrent queries. Which practices fit virtual threads? (Choose two.)

options.text: Start a new virtual thread per task, for example with `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`
options.why: Virtual threads are cheap; the JEP advises against pooling them.

options.text: Guard the database call with a `Semaphore` of 50 permits
options.why: A semaphore limits concurrency for the scarce resource without limiting threads.

options.text: Create a fixed pool of 50 virtual threads and reuse them for every task
options.why: Pooling virtual threads defeats their purpose; it just recreates a thread pool.

options.text: Call `Thread.yield()` before each query to slow the request rate
options.why: Yielding doesn't bound the number of in-flight queries.

options.text: Keep platform threads, because virtual threads cannot call JDBC
options.why: Virtual threads can run any blocking code, including JDBC.

explanation: JEP 444 recommends creating a virtual thread per task and never pooling them, because they are cheap. When the real constraint is a limited resource, such as database connections or a rate-limited API, limit concurrency at that resource with a `Semaphore` (or the connection pool), not by capping the number of threads.
reference: JEP 444: Virtual Threads ("Do not pool virtual threads")

options.text: Mark the `clients` field `volatile` so every thread sees the latest map
options.why: The map reference is already visible; the problem is the check-then-act gap.

options.text: Use `putIfAbsent(key, buildExpensiveClient(key))` instead of `put`
options.why: putIfAbsent is atomic, but the client is still built eagerly by every racing thread.

options.text: Use `computeIfAbsent(key, this::buildExpensiveClient)`
options.why: It runs the function at most once per absent key, atomically, and returns the value.

options.text: Wrap the map with `Collections.synchronizedMap`
options.why: Individual calls become synchronized, but the check and the put can still interleave.

explanation: Each `ConcurrentHashMap` method is thread-safe, but a sequence of calls is not atomic: two threads can both see the key missing and both build a client. `computeIfAbsent` performs the check and the insert atomically for that key and calls the function at most once. Keep the function short, and don't update other keys of the same map inside it.
reference: Java SE API: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent

stem: Four threads must increment one shared counter in Rust. Which type compiles and is correct?

options.text: `Rc<RefCell<i32>>`, cloned into each thread
options.why: Rc isn't Send and RefCell isn't Sync, so the compiler rejects it.

options.text: `Arc<RefCell<i32>>`, cloned into each thread
options.why: RefCell isn't Sync, so Arc<RefCell<_>> isn't Send and won't compile.

options.text: `Arc<Mutex<i32>>`, cloned into each thread
options.why: Arc shares ownership atomically and Mutex gives exclusive mutable access.

options.text: `Rc<Mutex<i32>>`, cloned into each thread
options.why: The Mutex is fine, but Rc's non-atomic count makes the whole type !Send.

explanation: `Arc<T>` is `Send` and `Sync` only when `T: Send + Sync`. `Mutex<T>` is `Sync` whenever `T: Send`, so `Arc<Mutex<i32>>` can be shared, and each thread locks to mutate. `RefCell` tracks borrows non-atomically and is `!Sync`, and `Rc` is `!Send`, so every alternative fails to compile. The compiler, not testing, rules out the data race.
reference: The Rust Book: Shared-State Concurrency

stem:
A worker thread panicked while holding the lock. What happens on the next line in another thread?

```rust
let guard = data.lock().unwrap();
```

options.text: It blocks forever, because the panicking thread never released the lock
options.why: Unwinding drops the guard, so the lock is released, but it is marked poisoned.

options.text: `lock()` returns `Err(PoisonError)`, so `unwrap()` panics
options.why: You can still recover the data with `into_inner()` on the error if it's safe.

options.text: `lock()` succeeds and hides the earlier panic completely
options.why: Rust surfaces the possibly inconsistent state through the Err variant.

options.text: The whole process aborts as soon as any thread panics
options.why: By default a thread panic unwinds that thread only.

explanation: When a thread panics while holding a `std::sync::Mutex`, unwinding drops the guard but marks the mutex poisoned. Later `lock()` calls return `Err(PoisonError)`, a signal that the protected data may be inconsistent. Calling `unwrap()` propagates the failure; to continue anyway, take the guard with `err.into_inner()` (or use `clear_poison`).
reference: Rust std::sync::Mutex: Poisoning

options.text: `tokio::spawn` forbids any kind of lock inside an async block
options.why: Locks are allowed; the issue is what lives across the .await.

options.text: The `std::sync::Mutex` itself is not `Send`
options.why: Mutex<T> is Send and Sync when T is Send; the guard is the problem.

options.text: `async move` blocks cannot capture variables from outside
options.why: Capturing with move is exactly what async move is for.

options.text: A `!Send` `MutexGuard` is held across `.await`
options.why: Drop the guard before awaiting, or use tokio::sync::Mutex if it must be held.

explanation: A future's state includes every value alive across an `.await`. `std::sync::MutexGuard` is `!Send`, so the whole future becomes `!Send`, and `tokio::spawn` requires `Send` futures because tasks can move between worker threads. Release the guard before the await (copy the needed data out), or use `tokio::sync::Mutex`, whose guard may be held across awaits.
reference: Tokio tutorial: Shared state (holding a MutexGuard across an .await)

stem: A Go program has a `jobs` channel feeding N worker goroutines that write to a `results` channel. Put the steps of a clean shutdown in order.

options.text: The producer calls `close(jobs)` after sending the last job
Each worker's `for j := range jobs` loop ends once the channel is drained
Each worker calls `wg.Done()` as it returns
`wg.Wait()` returns once every worker has finished
The coordinator calls `close(results)` so the consumer's range loop can end

explanation: Only the sender closes a channel, and only after its last send. Closing `jobs` lets each worker's `range` finish after draining the remaining jobs. Workers signal through the WaitGroup, and only after `Wait` returns is it safe to close `results`; closing it earlier would make a still-running worker panic with "send on closed channel".
reference: Go blog: Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation

stem: In an Erlang/OTP supervision tree, a `db_conn` process is started first, followed by three worker processes that all use it. If `db_conn` crashes, the workers must be restarted too. If one worker crashes, only that worker should restart. Which supervisor strategy fits?

options.text: `one_for_one`, restarting only the child that crashed
options.why: It restarts only the crashed child, so workers keep a dead connection when db_conn dies.

options.text: `one_for_all`, restarting every child after any crash
options.why: It restarts everything whenever any child crashes, including the healthy db_conn.

options.text: `rest_for_one`, with `db_conn` listed first
options.why: A crash restarts that child and every child started after it, matching the dependency order.

options.text: `simple_one_for_one`
options.why: That suits many identical, dynamically added children, not a dependency chain.

explanation: With `rest_for_one`, when a child terminates the supervisor restarts it and all children started after it. Listing `db_conn` first means its crash restarts the workers that depend on it, while a worker crash restarts only that worker and those after it. This is the "let it crash" idea: recover by restarting known-good state rather than defensive error handling.
reference: Erlang/OTP: Supervisor Behaviour (restart strategies)

options.text: Make the handler `async void` and `await GetDataAsync()` instead of using `.Result`
options.why: "Async all the way" means the UI thread is never blocked waiting.

options.text: Add `.ConfigureAwait(false)` to every `await` inside `GetDataAsync`
options.why: The continuation then runs on the thread pool, not the blocked UI thread.

options.text: Replace `.Result` with `.Wait()` and then read the result
options.why: Wait() blocks the UI thread in exactly the same way.

options.text: Raise the thread-pool minimum with `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads`
options.why: The continuation needs the UI thread specifically; more pool threads don't help.

options.text: Mark `GetDataAsync` as `async void` instead of `async Task`
options.why: Then there's nothing to await, and exceptions can crash the process.

explanation: The `await` in `GetDataAsync` captures the UI `SynchronizationContext`, so its continuation must run on the UI thread. But `.Result` blocks that thread waiting for the task, and each side waits for the other. Awaiting all the way up removes the block; `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code lets the continuation run on a pool thread. Event handlers are the one place `async void` is acceptable.
reference: Microsoft Learn: Async/Await best practices; ConfigureAwait FAQ

options.text: Add a `default:` case so the select never blocks
options.why: A default case turns the loop into a busy spin; that makes the CPU problem worse.

options.text: Use `v, ok := <-a`, and when `ok` is false set `a = nil`; same for `b`
options.why: A nil channel case is never ready, so select stops choosing the closed channel.

options.text: Close `out` as soon as either input channel closes
options.why: That loses the remaining values from the other channel and risks sends on a closed channel.

options.text: Wrap each receive in a `recover()` to catch the closed channel
options.why: Receiving from a closed channel doesn't panic, so recover catches nothing.

explanation: A closed channel is always ready to receive, returning zero values, so once `a` closes, select keeps picking it and spins. The loop condition never becomes false because nothing sets the variables to nil. Checking `ok` and setting the drained channel to `nil` disables that case permanently (a nil channel never becomes ready), and the loop ends once both are nil.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Select statements, Receive operator

stem: In Go, a buffered channel with capacity 1 used as `sem <- struct{}{}` before a critical section and `<-sem` after it provides both mutual exclusion and visibility: writes made inside one section are guaranteed visible in the next.

options.text: True
options.why: The memory model says the kth receive on a channel of capacity C happens before the (k+C)th send completes, so each section happens-before the next.

options.text: False
options.why: This is a documented guarantee of the Go memory model, not just a scheduling accident.

explanation: The Go memory model states that the kth receive on a channel with capacity C is synchronized before the completion of the (k+C)th send. With C = 1, the receive ending one critical section happens before the send starting the next, so the channel works as a mutex with full visibility. The same rule makes a capacity-N channel a counting semaphore.
reference: The Go Memory Model: Channel communication

stem: An HTTP service starts a background goroutine per request that does `for msg := range updates { ... }`, but the producer never closes `updates`. Memory climbs for days, yet the process never prints `all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. Why not?

options.text: The runtime only checks for deadlock during garbage collection
options.why: Detection isn't tied to GC; the condition is simply never met here.

options.text: Other goroutines, like the HTTP server, are still alive
options.why: The runtime only reports deadlock when every goroutine is blocked; leaked ones go unnoticed.

options.text: A `range` loop over a channel times out after 30 seconds by default
options.why: Range waits indefinitely for values or a close; there is no timeout.

options.text: Deadlock detection is disabled when GOMAXPROCS is greater than 1
options.why: GOMAXPROCS doesn't affect it.

explanation: The fatal deadlock error only fires when all goroutines are blocked and nothing can make progress. A server always has goroutines waiting on the network, so leaked goroutines blocked on channel receives are never reported. They pile up silently. Detect them with goroutine profiles (`pprof`, `runtime.NumGoroutine`) or tests using `goleak`, and fix them with explicit close or context cancellation.
reference: Go runtime: deadlock detection; net/http/pprof goroutine profile

stem: A Java service calls `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingHttpCall())` without an executor in several request paths. Under load, unrelated `parallelStream()` computations elsewhere in the app slow to a crawl. What is the root cause?

options.text: Parallel streams and futures are serialized by a global JVM lock
options.why: There is no such lock; they share a pool, not a lock.

options.text: Virtual threads are being created implicitly and exhaust carrier threads
options.why: supplyAsync without an executor uses platform threads from the common pool.

options.text: Both share `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which blocking calls exhaust
options.why: Pass a dedicated executor to supplyAsync for blocking work.

options.text: `supplyAsync` runs on the caller thread, blocking the request threads
options.why: It runs asynchronously, on the common pool by default.

explanation: `supplyAsync(supplier)` uses `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which by default has about one thread fewer than the CPU count and is shared with parallel streams. Blocking I/O in that pool occupies its threads, so CPU-bound parallel work queues behind it. Supply a separate executor sized for I/O, or a virtual-thread-per-task executor, for blocking calls.
reference: Java SE API: CompletableFuture (default async executor); ForkJoinPool.commonPool

stem: After moving from a 200-thread pool to one virtual thread per request (about 1 million live virtual threads at peak), a Java service runs out of heap. A library caches an expensive 2 MB parser object in a `ThreadLocal`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Virtual threads each reserve a fixed 1 MB stack on the heap
options.why: Virtual thread stacks grow and shrink on the heap; they are small when idle.

options.text: There is now one cached parser per virtual thread
options.why: ThreadLocal caching assumes a few long-lived threads; with millions it multiplies memory.

options.text: `ThreadLocal` values are copied to every carrier thread
options.why: Each virtual thread has its own ThreadLocal values; carriers don't copy them.

options.text: Virtual threads are never garbage-collected after they finish
options.why: Terminated virtual threads and their thread-locals become collectable.

explanation: Virtual threads fully support `ThreadLocal`, but each virtual thread has its own copy. Caching a heavy object per thread was cheap with 200 pooled threads; with a million short-lived virtual threads it creates up to a million parsers. JEP 444 warns against this pattern. Share an immutable or thread-safe instance, or use an explicit object pool.
reference: JEP 444: Virtual Threads (thread-local variables)

stem: Why is `Arc<Cell<i32>>` rejected when moved into `std::thread::spawn`, even though `Cell<i32>` is `Send`?

options.text: `Arc` requires the inner type to implement `Copy`
options.why: Arc has no Copy requirement; Cell<i32> is even Copy-able inside.

options.text: `Cell` can only hold heap-allocated types such as `Box`, not a plain `i32`
options.why: Cell works with any T; Cell<i32> is common.

options.text: `thread::spawn` never accepts `Arc` values
options.why: Arc is the standard way to share data with spawned threads.

options.text: `Arc<T>` is `Send` only if `T: Sync`, and `Cell` is `!Sync`
options.why: Cloned Arcs give several threads `&Cell`, and unsynchronized interior mutability would race.

explanation: `Arc<T>` implements `Send` (and `Sync`) only when `T: Send + Sync`, because cloning an `Arc` lets several threads obtain `&T` at once. `Cell<T>` allows mutation through a shared reference without synchronization, so it is `!Sync`. `Arc<Cell<i32>>` is therefore `!Send`. Use `Arc<AtomicI32>` or `Arc<Mutex<i32>>`.
reference: Rust std::sync::Arc (Send/Sync impls); std::cell::Cell

stem: Which problems does safe Rust's type system (ownership plus `Send`/`Sync`) rule out at compile time? (Choose two.)

options.text: Data races on shared memory
options.why: Shared mutable access across threads requires a Sync type such as Mutex or atomics.

options.text: Use-after-free from a thread touching data another thread freed
options.why: Ownership and lifetimes stop threads from outliving or freeing borrowed data.

options.text: Deadlocks from two threads taking two mutexes in opposite orders
options.why: Lock ordering is a logic issue; safe Rust happily compiles a deadlock.

options.text: Check-then-act race conditions across two separate lock acquisitions
options.why: Each access is synchronized, but the higher-level invariant can still break.

options.text: Memory leaks such as `Rc` reference cycles or `mem::forget`
options.why: Leaks are considered memory-safe in Rust and are not prevented.

explanation: Rust's guarantee is "no data races and no memory unsafety" in safe code. It does not prevent deadlocks, higher-level race conditions (for example, reading a balance under one lock and writing it under another), or memory leaks. Those still need design discipline, such as lock ordering, holding one lock across the whole invariant, and weak references.
reference: The Rustonomicon: Data Races and Race Conditions

stem: In an ASP.NET Core app (no `SynchronizationContext`), a controller calls `GetDataAsync().Result` on every request. The same code deadlocks in WPF, but here it doesn't. What is the real risk?

options.text: None: without a SynchronizationContext, `.Result` is as efficient as `await`
options.why: It doesn't deadlock, but it still blocks a pool thread for the whole call.

options.text: It deadlocks only on the first request, until the JIT warms up
options.why: Deadlock depends on a captured context, not on JIT warm-up.

options.text: It throws `InvalidOperationException` because `.Result` is banned there
options.why: The call is allowed; it just wastes threads.

options.text: Blocked pool threads cause thread-pool starvation under load
options.why: Continuations need pool threads too; blocked threads slow everything until the pool injects more.

explanation: Without a `SynchronizationContext`, continuations run on any thread-pool thread, so the classic UI deadlock doesn't occur. But `.Result` still blocks a pool thread for the full I/O duration, and the continuations that would complete those tasks also need pool threads. Under load the pool starves; it injects threads only slowly, and latency spikes. Use `await` all the way.
reference: Microsoft Learn: ASP.NET Core performance best practices (avoid blocking calls)

stem: An Erlang process receives with a pattern that matches only `{reply, Ref, _}` messages, while thousands of unrelated `{log, _}` messages pile up in its mailbox. Throughput collapses over time. Why?

options.text: Unmatched messages are resent to the sender, doubling the traffic
options.why: Messages stay in the receiver's mailbox; they are never bounced.

options.text: Each receive rescans every unmatched message in the mailbox
options.why: Handle or drop unexpected messages, or route them to another process.

options.text: The BEAM pauses the process until the mailbox is empty
options.why: The scheduler doesn't wait for an empty mailbox.

options.text: Erlang mailboxes have a fixed capacity, and senders block when it is full
options.why: Mailboxes are unbounded; the danger is unbounded growth, not blocking.

explanation: A selective `receive` walks the mailbox from the oldest message, skipping those that don't match. If unmatched messages accumulate, every receive does work proportional to the mailbox size, and the process slows while memory grows. Always include a catch-all clause that handles or discards unexpected messages; OTP behaviours do this with `handle_info`.
reference: Erlang Efficiency Guide: Processes (receiving messages)

stem: Match each language with a mechanism that publishes data written by one thread so another thread is guaranteed to see it.

options.text: A channel send that happens before the matching receive completes
options.why: Go's memory model defines happens-before through channel operations.

options.text: A write to a `volatile` field, followed by a read of it
options.why: The JMM orders a volatile write before subsequent reads of the same field.

options.text: An atomic store with `Release` paired with a load using `Acquire`
options.why: Rust follows the C++20 memory model for atomics.

options.text: `Atomics.store` and `Atomics.load` on a `SharedArrayBuffer`
options.why: Atomics operations are sequentially consistent between workers.

explanation: Every language needs a happens-before edge to make one thread's writes visible to another. Go provides it through channel operations (and sync primitives), Java through volatile and monitors, Rust through atomic orderings and its sync types, and JavaScript through `Atomics` operations on shared memory. Plain writes to shared memory give no such guarantee in any of them.
reference: The Go Memory Model; JLS §17.4; Rust std::sync::atomic::Ordering; ECMAScript memory model

options.text: `allOf` completes exceptionally after 100 ms and cancels `fa` and `fc`
options.why: allOf never cancels its inputs, and it waits for all of them to finish.

options.text: `join` throws only after about 30 s, once all three futures are done
options.why: allOf completes when all inputs complete; a and c keep running regardless.

options.text: `join` returns normally, because `allOf` ignores failed inputs
options.why: allOf completes exceptionally if any input failed.

options.text: It throws after 100 ms, but `a` and `c` are interrupted
options.why: Nothing interrupts them; CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt running tasks.

explanation: `allOf` returns a future that completes when all inputs have completed, exceptionally if any of them failed. It does not short-circuit or cancel the others, so the failure surfaces only after the slowest call finishes and the work keeps consuming resources. For fail-fast behaviour, attach a handler that cancels the siblings, or use structured concurrency, which cancels sibling subtasks when one fails.
reference: Java SE API: CompletableFuture.allOf

options.text: `errgroup` cancels only goroutines that started after the failure
options.why: errgroup cancels ctx for everyone; the goroutines just ignore it.

options.text: `g.Wait()` waits only for the first error and returns immediately
options.why: Wait blocks until every goroutine returns; that is why the call takes 30 s.

options.text: Each fetch gets `context.Background()`, not the group's `ctx`
options.why: Pass the group ctx into fetch so the first error cancels the others.

options.text: Loop variable `u` is shared, so all goroutines fetch the slowest URL
options.why: Since Go 1.22, each iteration has its own u.

explanation: `errgroup.WithContext` cancels the derived `ctx` when the first goroutine returns an error, and `Wait` returns that first error only after every goroutine has returned. Cancellation is cooperative: goroutines must pass `ctx` down to the I/O calls. Using `context.Background()` detaches them, so they run to completion and `Wait` blocks for the full 30 s.
reference: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup: WithContext, Group.Wait

options.text: A fresh config, because `Once` retries after a panic
options.why: Once does not retry; a panicking f still counts as done.

options.text: `nil`: `Do` counts the panicked call as done
options.why: Use sync.OnceValues, or your own error-aware logic, when initialization can fail.

options.text: It panics again with the same value on every call
options.why: That is the behaviour of sync.OnceFunc/OnceValue, not of a plain Once.Do.

options.text: It blocks forever, waiting for the first call to complete
options.why: The first call did return (by panicking), so later callers don't block.

explanation: The `sync` docs say that if `f` panics, `Do` considers it to have returned, and later calls of `Do` return without calling `f`. Because `cfg` was never assigned, it stays `nil` and later callers hit nil-pointer bugs. Go 1.21 added `sync.OnceFunc`, `OnceValue` and `OnceValues`, whose returned functions re-panic with the same value on every call, making the failure visible.
reference: Go package sync: Once.Do, OnceValue

stem: A team compares three servers that each run a request handler which accidentally spins in a pure CPU loop for 5 seconds. In which runtime do other concurrent requests on the same node keep being served promptly, without any code changes?

options.text: Node.js, because async functions yield to other requests on their own
options.why: Async functions only yield at await; a CPU loop blocks the whole event loop.

options.text: Python asyncio, because the event loop preempts long-running coroutines
options.why: asyncio is cooperative; a coroutine that never awaits blocks the loop.

options.text: Erlang/BEAM, which preempts each process after a budget of reductions
options.why: Schedulers switch processes preemptively, unless the time is spent in a long native NIF.

options.text: All three, because modern runtimes detect and pause CPU-heavy handlers
options.why: Only preemptive schedulers can interrupt code that never yields.

explanation: The BEAM schedulers preempt Erlang processes after they use a budget of reductions, so one busy process can't starve others on the same scheduler. Node.js and asyncio are cooperative: a callback or coroutine that never yields blocks every other request on that loop. The BEAM exception is native code (NIFs) that runs for long without yielding, which is why "dirty schedulers" exist. Go also preempts goroutines asynchronously since Go 1.14.
reference: Erlang docs: Scheduling (reductions); erl_nif dirty schedulers
